screens.title: Troubleshooting Chaincode and Transaction Failures
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to diagnose and resolve the most common chaincode and transaction failures in Hyperledger Fabric. You will see how to read peer and chaincode logs, identify which peer produced an error, and apply fixes such as correcting input validation, re-deploying chaincode, updating client targets, or implementing retry logic. Finally, we'll cover best practices: using debug-level logging, running unit and integration tests, and minimizing hot keys in your data model. By the end of this chapter you will know where failures occur in the transaction lifecycle, how to locate the source of the problem, and what pragmatic steps to take to restore correct behavior. screens.title: Where failures occur in the transaction lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the transaction lifecycle because locating the failure stage narrows your troubleshooting path. A Fabric transaction begins as a proposal from the client that endorsing peers execute to produce read-write sets. If the chaincode panics or returns an error during this execution, the peer will not endorse and the client will receive a chaincode execution error. If endorsement succeeds, the client collects endorsements and submits the proposal to the ordering service. A failure here looks like a missing endorsement set: the error indicates not enough endorsements. Finally, after ordering and block creation, validating peers check read-write sets against current ledger versions. If a key read during endorsement changed before commit, the transaction is marked INVALID with an MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. A concrete example: two clients read the same asset version; both propose updates; one commits and advances the version; the second fails validation. A common misconception is to treat all failures as chaincode bugs; many are policy or concurrency problems. The takeaway: determine whether the client received a chaincode error, an endorsement failure, or a validation invalidation, then apply the focused diagnostic steps for that stage.

keyIdea.title: Stage-based triage
keyIdea.text: Classify failures as execution, endorsement collection, or validation to pick the right diagnostic path quickly.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.8 › Transaction Lifecycle
Process: Proposal → Endorse → Order → Validate → Commit
Each step can produce failures with distinct signatures: chaincode errors during endorsement, endorsement collection errors, or MVCC invalidation at validation.
Diagnostic bullets
  • Chaincode execution error: client gets status 500 and descriptive message; check chaincode logs.
  • Endorsement failure: response reports not enough endorsements; check policy and peer targets.
  • Validation invalidation: transaction marked INVALID with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT in committer logs.
Key Takeaway

Triage by error signature: message content, endorsement count, or committer MVCC logs point to different fixes.

Example scenario
Two clients attempt to update the same asset concurrently. Both proposals are endorsed, the first is ordered and committed, and the second fails validation with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT when its read-set no longer matches ledger versions.
Check your understanding
If a client sees a 500 with "asset not found", which stage failed and where do you look first?

screens.title: Chaincode Execution Errors
screens.narratorSegment: A chaincode execution error happens when smart contract logic throws an error during endorsement. This appears as a status 500 returned to the client and usually contains the chaincode error string such as "asset not found" or "invalid input." The primary source of truth is the endorsing peer's logs and the chaincode container logs where fmt. Println or logger calls appear with a chaincode prefix. Concretely, when you see a client error, identify which peer responded with the endorsement; then check that peer's docker logs for the chaincode container. Common root causes include malformed JSON causing json. Unmarshal to fail, missing keys from GetState returning nil, or explicit business logic rejections. A typical misconception is to immediately redeploy chaincode without reading logs; redeploying can hide the original error and miss the needed code fix. A practical step sequence: reproduce the error, open the endorsing peer's logs, find the chaincode error string and stack context, fix the chaincode logic, run unit tests, then repackage and upgrade the chaincode. A final reflective question: what log line would prove the error was caused by an input validation failure versus a state access failure?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.8 › Chaincode Execution Errors
Definition
Errors raised by chaincode during endorsement, surfaced to the client and recorded in peer/container logs.
Diagnosis steps
  • Confirm which peer endorsed the failing proposal.
  • Run docker logs <peer_container> and docker logs <chaincode_container> to see chaincode output.
  • Search for the chaincode error string and stack context to find the code path.
Common mistake

Redeploying without reading logs can mask the original bug. Always map the error back to code first.

Concrete example
A client invokes UpdateAsset and gets "asset not found". Peer logs show a nil return from GetState and a custom error returned by the chaincode. Fix: add an existence check and clearer error handling, then redeploy.
Pro tip
Add targeted logger.Info statements around parsing and state access during development to capture inputs and state versions in logs.

screens.title: Endorsement Policy Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Endorsement policy failures happen when a proposal does not collect the set of endorsements specified by the chaincode's policy. The policy might require endorsements from specific organizations or combinations, for example AND('Org1MSP. peer','Org2MSP. peer') or OR('Org1MSP. peer','Org2MSP. peer'). A common error message reports failed to get enough endorsements with counts such as required 2, got 1. To diagnose, confirm the policy expression, check that all required peers are online and have joined the channel, and verify that each required peer has the correct chaincode package and approved definition. Also inspect the client application configuration: many SDKs allow specifying target peers, and sending the proposal to only one peer when two are required results in a shortfall. A common misconception is to change the policy immediately. Instead, first check peer health and installation because the simplest causes are an offline peer or missing approval. Example: if Org2's peer crashed, the client will only receive Org1's endorsement and the transaction will fail. The corrective actions include bringing peers back online, installing/approving chaincode on missing peers, or carefully updating the endorsement policy via a chaincode definition upgrade if the policy itself was incorrect.

keyIdea.title: Endorsement troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Verify policy, peer health, installed chaincode versions, and that the client targets all required endorsers before changing policy.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.8 › Endorsement Policy Failures
What to check
  • Policy expression and required organizations.
  • Peer availability and whether they joined the channel.
  • Chaincode installed/approved versions on required peers.
  • Client proposal target list includes all required endorsers.
Common cause

A required peer is down or has not approved the chaincode definition; the client only gets partial endorsements and the proposal fails.

Concrete example
Policy AND('Org1MSP.peer','Org2MSP.peer') but Org2's peer crashed. Client gets only Org1 endorsement and sees "required 2, got 1". Restore Org2 or adjust client targets.
Resolution checklist
  1. Check docker ps and peer logs for offline peers.
  2. Verify chaincode install and approval on required peers.
  3. Confirm client proposal targets include all required peers.

screens.title: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) Conflicts
screens.narratorSegment: MVCC ensures ledger consistency by checking that the versions of keys read during endorsement still match at commit time. When endorsing peers execute chaincode they record the versions of keys read into a read-set. Later, validating peers compare those versions to the current ledger state. If any key was modified by a previously committed transaction, the read-set is stale and the transaction is invalidated with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. A concrete analogy: two people edit the same paragraph in a shared document. The first save succeeds; the second save, based on the earlier version, is rejected because the content changed. In Fabric, the rejected transaction is marked INVALID and its writes are discarded, avoiding lost updates. A common misconception is to think MVCC indicates a chaincode bug — it is usually a concurrency artifact. To mitigate, redesign data to avoid hot keys by sharding counters or using per-user keys, implement client retry with backoff and re-read of the latest state before resubmitting, or serialize operations at the application layer when appropriate. The key takeaway: MVCC is a consistency safety net; reduce contention and add retry handling to maintain throughput.

keyIdea.title: MVCC essence
keyIdea.text: MVCC invalidations protect against lost updates by rejecting transactions whose read-set was changed before commit; handle with data design and retries.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.8 › MVCC Conflicts
What is MVCC_READ_CONFLICT?
Validation failure when a transaction's read-set versions no longer match ledger versions because another transaction modified those keys first.
Symptoms & Diagnosis
  • Transaction appears endorsed but is marked INVALID on the ledger.
  • Peer committer logs show MVCC_READ_CONFLICT for the transaction ID.
  • Often occurs on hot keys with many concurrent updates.
Analogy
Like saving a shared document: if someone else saved first, your update conflicts with the new version and must be retried based on the updated state.
Key Takeaway

Treat MVCC as an expected concurrency control signal; respond with data design changes or retries rather than code panics.

screens.title: Hands-on: Inducing an MVCC Conflict
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on flow demonstrates how MVCC conflicts appear in practice. First, bring up a clean test network and deploy the asset-transfer chaincode. Then initialize an asset named assetHot to create a hot key that multiple clients will update. Next, open two terminals and run two update invokes against assetHot within a second of each other. One invoke will be ordered and committed, the other will either fail during endorsement or be invalidated at commit with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. Observe peer docker logs for committer messages showing the invalidation. A concrete example command sequence is provided in the visual code block for you to run. A common error is running invokes too slowly; to reliably induce conflict you must start both commands almost simultaneously. The learning point is not to break the network but to see how a valid endorsement can still produce an invalid ledger entry in the second transaction and to learn how to detect that invalidation in logs and queries. After the experiment, query the asset to confirm which update persisted and inspect logs to locate the MVCC message. What would you change in your application to avoid this conflict?

screens.title: Interpreting Peer and Chaincode Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Reading logs is the fastest way to locate chaincode and transaction issues. Peer logs will include modules such as [chaincode] and [committer] which point to execution and validation activities. When a chaincode returns an error during endorsement you will see the chaincode container output with messages you placed in logger. Info or fmt. Println. For MVCC conflicts look for committer logs that say Transaction is invalid: MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. For endorsement problems, the peer logs may show failed endorsement attempts or timeout errors. A concrete example: after an MVCC invalidation you might see a committer debug line describing validation for a block and then a line showing the transaction was invalid with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT; the surrounding context will include the transaction ID and block number. A common pitfall is scanning only the client error string and not retrieving the peer logs from the endorsing peer; endorsements can come from different peers, so confirm which peer produced the endorsement and check that peer's logs. Practice: correlate the client error, the endorsing peer container logs, and the committer messages — that triple confirms whether you need a code fix, a peer health fix, or an application-level retry. How might you automate extracting transaction IDs from logs to speed repeated debugging?

keyIdea.text: Correlate client errors, endorsing peer/container logs, and committer messages to determine whether to fix code, peers, or application logic.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.8 › Logs & Interpretation
Key log markers
  • [chaincode] or chaincode container output → execution errors and logger messages.
  • [endorser] → proposal handling and endorsement decisions.
  • [committer] → validation and MVCC checks, where MVCC_READ_CONFLICT appears.
Practical technique
When a client error occurs, copy the transaction ID, then search peer logs for that ID to find endorsement and validation entries. This links the client symptom to the peer-level cause.
Example log snippet
[committer] validateAndCommitBlock -> DEBU 10f Validating transaction tx123 for block [7]...
[committer] validateAndCommitBlock -> DEBU 10g Transaction tx123 is invalid: MVCC_READ_CONFLICT
[chaincode] ERROR: asset not found while handling UpdateAsset
Use these lines to decide: MVCC invalidation or chaincode execution error?
Check your understanding

If a chaincode ERROR appears but the committer shows MVCC conflict for the same txid, which happened first and which error do you fix?

screens.title: Resolving MVCC: Application Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: MVCC conflicts are primarily an application design problem when many concurrent transactions target the same ledger key. To reduce conflicts, first identify hot keys — keys that receive frequent concurrent updates. A common mitigation is sharding the logical resource, for example using per-user keys or appending a time-slice to a counter so updates operate on different keys. If sharding is not feasible, implement client-side retry with exponential backoff: when receiving an MVCC_READ_CONFLICT, re-read the latest state, recompute your updates, and resubmit. Also minimize unnecessary GetState calls in chaincode, as extra reads enlarge the read-set and increase the chance of conflicts. For highly contentious operations consider batching or sequencing at the application layer so a single coordinator serializes updates. A misconception is to think optimistic concurrency alone will handle heavy contention; optimistic patterns work well under moderate concurrency but will produce many conflicts under very high load. A practical example: instead of a single global counter key, use counters per user or per shard index based on hashing; aggregate values when needed. The core takeaway: design to reduce overlapping read-sets and add robust retry logic to handle inevitable conflicts.

The core takeaway: design to reduce overlapping read-sets and add robust retry logic to handle inevitable conflicts.

keyIdea.text: Avoid hot keys by sharding or sequencing and use retries with re-read to recover from MVCC conflicts when they occur.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.8 › Resolving MVCC
Sharding example
Instead of key: totalCount, use keys like totalCount_2026_09_25 or totalCount_user123 so concurrent updates touch different keys and reduce read-set collisions.
Retry pattern
On MVCC error: wait a short backoff, re-query the current state, recompute the intended change, and resubmit the transaction. Use jitter to avoid retry storms.
Design checklist
  • Find hot keys and evaluate sharding by user or time window.
  • Reduce chaincode read-set size by avoiding unnecessary GetState calls.
  • Implement client retries with backoff and state re-read.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These concise definitions summarize the chapter's core concepts for quick review. Remember that a chaincode execution error is an error during endorsement returned by the chaincode logic and visible in peer or chaincode container logs. An endorsement policy failure occurs when a transaction cannot collect the required endorsements according to the policy expression; typically the cause is an offline peer, mismatched chaincode versions, or incorrect client targeting. MVCC conflict describes a transaction invalidated at validation because the read-set versions changed after endorsement. The read-write set is the specific keys read and written by a transaction; it is the data used by MVCC to validate transactions. Hot keys are ledger keys with high concurrent access and are common sources of MVCC conflicts. Keep these definitions handy when you read logs and decide whether to fix code, peers, or application design.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to diagnose and resolve the most common chaincode and transaction failures in Hyperledger Fabric. We'll focus on three practical areas: chaincode execution errors that show up during endorsement, endorsement policy failures that stop a proposal from collecting required endorsements, and MVCC read conflicts that cause valid-looking proposals to be invalidated at commit time. You will see how to read peer and chaincode logs, identify which peer produced an error, and apply fixes such as correcting input validation, re-deploying chaincode, updating client targets, or implementing retry logic. A hands-on MVCC activity demonstrates how two simultaneous updates to the same ledger key cause one transaction to be invalidated and how to interpret committer logs. Finally, we'll cover best practices: using debug-level logging, running unit and integration tests, and minimizing hot keys in your data model. By the end of this chapter you will know where failures occur in the transaction lifecycle, how to locate the source of the problem, and what pragmatic steps to take to restore correct behavior. Which failure mode would you want to practice first?

These objectives guide focused practice so you can troubleshoot chaincode and transaction failures confidently. First, you will diagnose common chaincode execution errors and transaction invalidation reasons by reading peer and chaincode logs and interpreting the client error strings. A concrete skill is locating an error string in peer docker logs and mapping it back to the chaincode line that produced it. Second, you will use chaincode and peer logs for debugging: identify the endorsing peer, inspect chaincode container logs, and attach a debugger in development scenarios. Third, you will understand endorsement policy failures: check policy expressions, peer health, whether required peers have installed and approved the chaincode, and whether the client targeted all required endorsers. Fourth, you will identify and resolve MVCC conflicts by recognizing read-write set mismatches, minimizing hot keys through data sharding, and implementing client-side retry strategies. Each objective pairs a practical action with why it matters so you can triage failures quickly and restore correct ledger state with minimal disruption.

This second objectives slide focuses on actionable debugging practices and safe production techniques. You will learn to increase peer logging with the FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC environment variable for short troubleshooting windows, attach a debugger in development for Go chaincode, and prefer unit and integration tests to find logic errors early. The narration will also cover safe re-deploy procedures — package, install, approve, and commit the chaincode definition — because careless upgrades can create endorsement mismatches. You will practice identifying hot keys in your data model and redesigning to shard state by user or time slice to avoid MVCC contention. Finally, you will implement client retry strategies with exponential backoff and re-read of state before resubmitting. These habits reduce operational risk, let you diagnose problems quickly, and make production troubleshooting faster and less disruptive.

Start by understanding the transaction lifecycle because locating the failure stage narrows your troubleshooting path. A Fabric transaction begins as a proposal from the client that endorsing peers execute to produce read-write sets. If the chaincode panics or returns an error during this execution, the peer will not endorse and the client will receive a chaincode execution error. If endorsement succeeds, the client collects endorsements and submits the proposal to the ordering service. A failure here looks like a missing endorsement set: the error indicates not enough endorsements. Finally, after ordering and block creation, validating peers check read-write sets against current ledger versions. If a key read during endorsement changed before commit, the transaction is marked INVALID with an MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. A concrete example: two clients read the same asset version; both propose updates; one commits and advances the version; the second fails validation. A common misconception is to treat all failures as chaincode bugs; many are policy or concurrency problems. The takeaway: determine whether the client received a chaincode error, an endorsement failure, or a validation invalidation, then apply the focused diagnostic steps for that stage.

A chaincode execution error happens when smart contract logic throws an error during endorsement. This appears as a status 500 returned to the client and usually contains the chaincode error string such as "asset not found" or "invalid input." The primary source of truth is the endorsing peer's logs and the chaincode container logs where fmt. Println or logger calls appear with a chaincode prefix. Concretely, when you see a client error, identify which peer responded with the endorsement; then check that peer's docker logs for the chaincode container. Common root causes include malformed JSON causing json. Unmarshal to fail, missing keys from GetState returning nil, or explicit business logic rejections. A typical misconception is to immediately redeploy chaincode without reading logs; redeploying can hide the original error and miss the needed code fix. A practical step sequence: reproduce the error, open the endorsing peer's logs, find the chaincode error string and stack context, fix the chaincode logic, run unit tests, then repackage and upgrade the chaincode. A final reflective question: what log line would prove the error was caused by an input validation failure versus a state access failure?

Endorsement policy failures happen when a proposal does not collect the set of endorsements specified by the chaincode's policy. The policy might require endorsements from specific organizations or combinations, for example AND('Org1MSP. peer','Org2MSP. peer') or OR('Org1MSP. peer','Org2MSP. peer'). A common error message reports failed to get enough endorsements with counts such as required 2, got 1. To diagnose, confirm the policy expression, check that all required peers are online and have joined the channel, and verify that each required peer has the correct chaincode package and approved definition. Also inspect the client application configuration: many SDKs allow specifying target peers, and sending the proposal to only one peer when two are required results in a shortfall. A common misconception is to change the policy immediately. Instead, first check peer health and installation because the simplest causes are an offline peer or missing approval. Example: if Org2's peer crashed, the client will only receive Org1's endorsement and the transaction will fail. The corrective actions include bringing peers back online, installing/approving chaincode on missing peers, or carefully updating the endorsement policy via a chaincode definition upgrade if the policy itself was incorrect.

MVCC ensures ledger consistency by checking that the versions of keys read during endorsement still match at commit time. When endorsing peers execute chaincode they record the versions of keys read into a read-set. Later, validating peers compare those versions to the current ledger state. If any key was modified by a previously committed transaction, the read-set is stale and the transaction is invalidated with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. A concrete analogy: two people edit the same paragraph in a shared document. The first save succeeds; the second save, based on the earlier version, is rejected because the content changed. In Fabric, the rejected transaction is marked INVALID and its writes are discarded, avoiding lost updates. A common misconception is to think MVCC indicates a chaincode bug — it is usually a concurrency artifact. To mitigate, redesign data to avoid hot keys by sharding counters or using per-user keys, implement client retry with backoff and re-read of the latest state before resubmitting, or serialize operations at the application layer when appropriate. The key takeaway: MVCC is a consistency safety net; reduce contention and add retry handling to maintain throughput.

This hands-on flow demonstrates how MVCC conflicts appear in practice. First, bring up a clean test network and deploy the asset-transfer chaincode. Then initialize an asset named assetHot to create a hot key that multiple clients will update. Next, open two terminals and run two update invokes against assetHot within a second of each other. One invoke will be ordered and committed, the other will either fail during endorsement or be invalidated at commit with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. Observe peer docker logs for committer messages showing the invalidation. A concrete example command sequence is provided in the visual code block for you to run. A common error is running invokes too slowly; to reliably induce conflict you must start both commands almost simultaneously. The learning point is not to break the network but to see how a valid endorsement can still produce an invalid ledger entry in the second transaction and to learn how to detect that invalidation in logs and queries. After the experiment, query the asset to confirm which update persisted and inspect logs to locate the MVCC message. What would you change in your application to avoid this conflict?

Reading logs is the fastest way to locate chaincode and transaction issues. Peer logs will include modules such as [chaincode] and [committer] which point to execution and validation activities. When a chaincode returns an error during endorsement you will see the chaincode container output with messages you placed in logger. Info or fmt. Println. For MVCC conflicts look for committer logs that say Transaction is invalid: MVCC_READ_CONFLICT. For endorsement problems, the peer logs may show failed endorsement attempts or timeout errors. A concrete example: after an MVCC invalidation you might see a committer debug line describing validation for a block and then a line showing the transaction was invalid with MVCC_READ_CONFLICT; the surrounding context will include the transaction ID and block number. A common pitfall is scanning only the client error string and not retrieving the peer logs from the endorsing peer; endorsements can come from different peers, so confirm which peer produced the endorsement and check that peer's logs. Practice: correlate the client error, the endorsing peer container logs, and the committer messages — that triple confirms whether you need a code fix, a peer health fix, or an application-level retry. How might you automate extracting transaction IDs from logs to speed repeated debugging?

MVCC conflicts are primarily an application design problem when many concurrent transactions target the same ledger key. To reduce conflicts, first identify hot keys — keys that receive frequent concurrent updates. A common mitigation is sharding the logical resource, for example using per-user keys or appending a time-slice to a counter so updates operate on different keys. If sharding is not feasible, implement client-side retry with exponential backoff: when receiving an MVCC_READ_CONFLICT, re-read the latest state, recompute your updates, and resubmit. Also minimize unnecessary GetState calls in chaincode, as extra reads enlarge the read-set and increase the chance of conflicts. For highly contentious operations consider batching or sequencing at the application layer so a single coordinator serializes updates. A misconception is to think optimistic concurrency alone will handle heavy contention; optimistic patterns work well under moderate concurrency but will produce many conflicts under very high load. A practical example: instead of a single global counter key, use counters per user or per shard index based on hashing; aggregate values when needed. The core takeaway: design to reduce overlapping read-sets and add robust retry logic to handle inevitable conflicts.

Remember that a chaincode execution error is an error during endorsement returned by the chaincode logic and visible in peer or chaincode container logs. An endorsement policy failure occurs when a transaction cannot collect the required endorsements according to the policy expression; typically the cause is an offline peer, mismatched chaincode versions, or incorrect client targeting. MVCC conflict describes a transaction invalidated at validation because the read-set versions changed after endorsement. The read-write set is the specific keys read and written by a transaction; it is the data used by MVCC to validate transactions. Hot keys are ledger keys with high concurrent access and are common sources of MVCC conflicts.
